newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia puts stress on economy ahead of poll.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia puts stress on economy ahead of poll.

text.p: Slovenia's economy topped the agenda in campaigning on Tuesday for the country's second general election.

While the Alpine former Yugoslav republic of two million people has made much progress in transforming its once-communist economy since gaining independence in 1991, opposition politicians blamed the ruling Liberal Democrats for failing to hold down inflation and unemployment.
The jobless, now about 7.5 percent of the work force, should be a top priority for the next government, the opposition United List of Social Democrats, the former communists, said.
Inflation rose to an annual 9.7 percent last month, despite government attempts to reduce the figure to six percent by year-end, partly because of a wave of strikes over higher pay.
"A successful economy should be based on social justice," United List leader Janez Kocijancic told a news conference.

The United List, along with the rightist Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party are bidding for votes on Sunday against Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats and their coalition partners, the Christian Democrats.

But Drnovsek, a former president of the now-defunct Yugoslav federation, has pinned his hopes for a fresh term of office on Slovenians' rising living standards and the country's strong prospects for closer integration with the western institutions, such as NATO and the European Union.
"We have been successfully implementing our economic policy for the past four years," Drnovsek told Slovenian television.

Slovenia hopes to join the EU in 2001 following an association agreement it signed with the 15-member bloc in June, and is considered a strong candidate for early membership in the North Atlantic military alliance.
The 1.5 million voters will have a choice among 28 parties, 10 of which are expected to win seats in parliament.
Opinion polls show the Liberal Democrats ahead with up to 21.8 percent of votes, followed by the People's Party with nine percent and the Social Democrats with eight percent.
Support for the United List was around six percent with a third of voters still undecided.
